summary: Describes the portion of fault isolation and recovery that is the responsibility of the host. This RFC is historic. Replaced by RFC 7805.

plainLanguage.summary: When something on the network breaks, each computer must do its part to find and fix the problem. This memo explains what the host's part is.

questions: how do hosts detect network failures
subtitle: How hosts detect and recover from network faults.

tldr.problem: When networks or gateways fail, the communication path must change, and hosts need to detect and recover from these failures.
tldr.mechanism: Hosts rely on gateways for routing advice via ICMP messages, and use strategies like polling, triggered reselection, or error message interpretation to detect and recover from faults.
tldr.outcome: This RFC defined the host's responsibilities in fault recovery; it is now historic and obsoleted by RFC 7805.

today: RFC 816 is Historic. It has been obsoleted by RFC 7805.

sections.title: The Problem of Network Failures
sections.content:
Fault isolation is the collective action of hosts and gateways to determine that something is wrong in the network. Fault recovery is the selection of an alternative route to reconnect source and destination. While gateways perform most of the fault isolation and recovery, hosts have their own responsibilities.

This RFC describes what hosts must do when networks or gateways fail. Because gateways maintain a consistent model of network topology, a host's strategy is simple: trust the gateway's advice when something goes wrong, and switch to another gateway if the current one is down.
sections.plainLanguage: When the network breaks, your computer must help figure out what is wrong and find a new path. The gateways in the middle do most of the work, but your computer has to do its part too.

sections.title: Gateway Topology Discovery
sections.content:
Gateways collectively implement an algorithm that identifies the best route between all pairs of networks by exchanging packets containing each gateway's opinion of which neighbor networks and gateways are operational. After a network or gateway failure, gateways go through a period of confusion as they negotiate new topology information, but eventually converge on a consistent and correct model of connectivity.

However, this convergence may take several minutes, longer than the timeout of many TCP implementations. The design goal is for gateways to reconstruct topology quickly enough that TCP connections can survive a route failure. Hosts should be aware that ICMP error messages arriving during this transient period may not accurately represent the network state.
sections.plainLanguage: Gateways talk to each other and figure out the best path between networks. When a path breaks, they chat to find a new one. But this takes a moment, so your computer should not trust error messages right away.

sections.title: Host Recovery Strategies
sections.content:
A host can detect a failed gateway through several strategies. Network level detection occurs when the underlying network itself (such as the Arpanet) notifies the host that a gateway is unreachable. Continuous polling uses ICMP Echo to query the gateway periodically, but this creates high overhead and is only suitable where overhead is analyzed and acceptable.

Triggered polling restricts polling to times when something seems wrong, such as when TCP retransmits, and avoids excessive overhead but may slow fault detection. Triggered reselection is the most elegant approach: when an upper layer hints at trouble, the IP layer simply switches to the next gateway in the list. If that gateway is up, correct results or ICMP advice follows; if wrong, a redirect message brings the host back to the original gateway.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer can detect a dead gateway several ways: wait for the network to tell it, ask the gateway repeatedly, ask when something looks wrong, or just try another gateway and see what happens.

sections.title: Finding and Selecting Gateways
sections.content:
A critical challenge is that the Internet Protocol specification does not define a standard message for hosts to request a list of available gateways. Different networks provide different discovery mechanisms: broadcast networks may have gateways broadcast their tables periodically; logical addressing may allow queries to a group address; or a host may build its table by remembering all gateways from which it has received messages. As a last resort, manual configuration by an operator may be required.

Once a host determines that its current gateway is down, it selects another gateway from its list and retries. The host must be prepared to apply its fault detection algorithm continuously as it tries each gateway in turn. If all known gateways are down, the situation is unrecoverable without manual intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: Your computer needs to know which gateways exist, but nobody defined a standard way to ask. Different networks do it differently—some gateways broadcast themselves, some you ask in a group, some you discover by listening, and some you just type in by hand.

sections.title: Interpreting ICMP Error Messages
sections.content:
Hosts receive ICMP advisory messages: a redirect indicates the current gateway is not the best choice for the destination, so the host should update its routing table; destination unreachable indicates the addressed network or host is currently unreachable, so the host can abandon the connection or wait. However, transient period errors may be unreliable, and hosts must interpret them with skepticism.

Error messages serve important purposes: they indicate problems when opening new connections, they provide evidence of failure reasons after TCP timeout, and they may signal implementation bugs. A combination of TCP timeout (a sure sign of serious trouble) and advisory error messages (context about what went wrong) provides the client layer with good facts for deciding how to respond. All error messages from all protocol layers should be passed up to the client module consistently.
sections.plainLanguage: The network sends back messages saying things like 'try a different gateway' or 'that place is broken right now.' But these messages might be wrong during a failure, so do not trust them alone. Wait for your timer to run out first.

sections.title: Application and TCP Responsibilities
sections.content:
TCP should detect prolonged connection failures via a configurable timeout and report timeouts to its client, allowing human-interactive clients (like Telnet) to see error messages and decide when to abort. Application-level fault detection is also required, because the foreign TCP peer may fail while TCP data is still being acknowledged, or the communication path may fail while no data is being sent.

SMTP mailers must set timeouts at the application level proportional to message size to avoid false alarms on large transfers. Telnet servers should use occasional queries when the user is idle to detect dead connections, but only triggered by detected idleness to avoid overwhelming the network. Fundamentally, application programmers must be aware of failure modes and understand that error detection at lower layers cannot solve the entire problem for them.
sections.plainLanguage: Your email program and chat app must also watch for problems on their own, because the low-level network might be working fine while the far end crashes. Apps need to pick their own timeouts and strategies based on what makes sense for them.
